lessons.title: Qiskit Architecture Overview
lessons.content:
Qiskit Architecture Overview

💡 What You'll Learn

Understand the modular architecture of IBM's Qiskit SDK, its core components, and how they work together to build and execute quantum programs.

What is Qiskit?

Qiskit (Quantum Information Science Kit) is IBM's open-source SDK for working with quantum computers. It provides tools for creating quantum circuits, running simulations, and executing on real quantum hardware.

Core Components

Qiskit Terra

The foundation layer providing circuit building, transpilation, and quantum information tools.

  • QuantumCircuit class
  • Transpiler framework
  • Quantum operators

Qiskit Aer

High-performance quantum circuit simulators with noise modeling.

  • Statevector simulator
  • QASM simulator
  • Noise models

Modern Qiskit Structure

# Modern Qiskit imports (v1.0+)
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector, Operator
from qiskit.primitives import Sampler, Estimator
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService

# Create a simple circuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure_all()

print(qc.draw())

Execution Flow

  1. 1
    Build - Create quantum circuits using QuantumCircuit
  2. 2
    Transpile - Optimize circuits for target backend
  3. 3
    Execute - Run on simulator or real quantum hardware
  4. 4
    Analyze - Process results and extract insights
keyTakeaways: Qiskit is IBM's open-source quantum computing SDK
Core components: Terra (circuits), Aer (simulators), IBM Runtime (hardware)
Modern Qiskit uses Primitives (Sampler, Estimator) for execution
The workflow is: Build → Transpile → Execute → Analyze

codeExamples.code:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

# Create a 2-qubit circuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)      # Hadamard on qubit 0
qc.cx(0, 1)  # CNOT
qc.measure_all()

print(qc.draw())

lessons.title: QuantumCircuit & QuantumRegister
lessons.content:
QuantumCircuit & QuantumRegister

🔬 Hands-On Lab

In this lab, you'll master the fundamental building blocks of Qiskit: QuantumCircuit and QuantumRegister classes.

Creating Quantum Circuits

The QuantumCircuit class is the core container for quantum operations in Qiskit.

# Method 1: Simple creation
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(3)  # 3 qubits, no classical bits
qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)  # 3 qubits, 3 classical bits

# Method 2: Using registers
from qiskit import QuantumRegister, ClassicalRegister

qr = QuantumRegister(2, 'q')  # Named quantum register
cr = ClassicalRegister(2, 'c')  # Named classical register
qc = QuantumCircuit(qr, cr)

Working with Multiple Registers

# Multiple quantum registers for organization
data = QuantumRegister(3, 'data')
ancilla = QuantumRegister(1, 'ancilla')
output = ClassicalRegister(3, 'output')

qc = QuantumCircuit(data, ancilla, output)

# Apply gates to specific registers
qc.h(data[0])
qc.cx(data[0], data[1])
qc.x(ancilla[0])
qc.measure(data, output)

Circuit Properties

qc.num_qubits

Total number of qubits

qc.num_clbits

Total classical bits

qc.depth()

Circuit depth (layers)

qc.size()

Total gate count

Try It Yourself

# Exercise: Create a 3-qubit GHZ state circuit
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)

# Your code here:
# 1. Apply H to qubit 0
# 2. Apply CNOT from 0 to 1
# 3. Apply CNOT from 1 to 2
# 4. Measure all qubits

qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.cx(1, 2)
qc.measure_all()

print(qc.draw())
print(f"Depth: {qc.depth()}, Size: {qc.size()}")
keyTakeaways: QuantumCircuit is the main container for quantum programs
Use QuantumRegister and ClassicalRegister for organized circuits
Circuit properties: num_qubits, depth(), size(), count_ops()
Multiple registers help organize complex algorithms

codeExamples.code:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, QuantumRegister, ClassicalRegister

qr = QuantumRegister(2, 'q')
cr = ClassicalRegister(2, 'c')
qc = QuantumCircuit(qr, cr)

qc.h(qr[0])
qc.cx(qr[0], qr[1])
qc.measure(qr, cr)

print(qc.draw())

lessons.title: The Aer Simulator
lessons.content:
The Aer Simulator

🔬 Hands-On Lab

Learn to use Qiskit Aer for high-performance quantum circuit simulation with various backend options.

What is Qiskit Aer?

Qiskit Aer provides high-performance simulators for quantum circuits. It's essential for developing and testing quantum algorithms before running on real hardware.

Simulator Types

AerSimulator

General-purpose simulator supporting multiple methods

Statevector

Full quantum state simulation

QASM

Measurement-based simulation

Basic Usage

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator

# Create a Bell state circuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure_all()

# Create simulator and run
simulator = AerSimulator()
transpiled = transpile(qc, simulator)
job = simulator.run(transpiled, shots=1024)
result = job.result()
counts = result.get_counts()

print(counts)  # {'00': ~512, '11': ~512}

Simulation Methods

# Statevector method (exact simulation)
sim_statevector = AerSimulator(method='statevector')

# Matrix product state (for certain circuits)
sim_mps = AerSimulator(method='matrix_product_state')

# Density matrix (for noise simulation)
sim_density = AerSimulator(method='density_matrix')

# Automatic method selection (default)
sim_auto = AerSimulator(method='automatic')

Getting the Statevector

from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector

# Create circuit WITHOUT measurement
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)

# Get exact statevector
state = Statevector.from_instruction(qc)
print(state.draw('text'))

# Output: [0.707+0j, 0, 0, 0.707+0j]
# This is |00⟩ + |11⟩ (Bell state)
keyTakeaways: Qiskit Aer provides high-performance quantum simulators
AerSimulator supports multiple simulation methods
Use transpile() before running on any backend
Statevector gives exact quantum state, counts give measurement statistics

codeExamples.code:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure_all()

sim = AerSimulator()
result = sim.run(transpile(qc, sim), shots=1000).result()
print(result.get_counts())

lessons.title: Transpiler Pipeline
lessons.content:
Transpiler Pipeline

💡 Why Transpilation?

Real quantum hardware has constraints: limited connectivity, specific gate sets, and noise. The transpiler converts your abstract circuit into one that can run on actual hardware.

What is Transpilation?

Transpilation is the process of transforming a quantum circuit to match the constraints of a specific backend (simulator or real device). This includes:

  • Basis translation: Convert gates to the backend's native gate set
  • Layout mapping: Map virtual qubits to physical qubits
  • Routing: Add SWAP gates for non-adjacent qubit interactions
  • Optimization: Reduce circuit depth and gate count

Transpiler Stages

  1. 1
    Init - Unroll custom gates, check validity
  2. 2
    Layout - Map virtual qubits → physical qubits
  3. 3
    Routing - Insert SWAPs for connectivity
  4. 4
    Translation - Convert to basis gates (CX, RZ, SX, X)
  5. 5
    Optimization - Simplify and reduce gate count
  6. 6
    Scheduling - Add timing for pulses (optional)

Basic Transpilation

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator

# Original circuit with Toffoli gate
qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.h(0)
qc.ccx(0, 1, 2)  # Toffoli - not a basis gate!
qc.measure_all()

print("Original:")
print(qc.draw())
print(f"Depth: {qc.depth()}, Gates: {qc.size()}")

# Transpile for simulator
backend = AerSimulator()
transpiled = transpile(qc, backend, optimization_level=1)

print("\nTranspiled:")
print(transpiled.draw())
print(f"Depth: {transpiled.depth()}, Gates: {transpiled.size()}")

Optimization Levels

optimization_level=0

No optimization. Just mapping and basis translation.

optimization_level=1

Light optimization. Good balance of speed and quality.

optimization_level=2

Medium optimization. Better results, more time.

optimization_level=3

Heavy optimization. Best results, slowest.

# Compare optimization levels
for level in [0, 1, 2, 3]:
    t = transpile(qc, backend, optimization_level=level)
    print(f"Level {level}: depth={t.depth()}, gates={t.size()}")
keyTakeaways: Transpilation converts circuits to match hardware constraints
Stages: Init → Layout → Routing → Translation → Optimization
optimization_level controls the trade-off between speed and quality
Always transpile before running on real hardware

codeExamples.code:
from qiskit import transpile

# Transpile with different optimization levels
for level in [0, 1, 2, 3]:
    tc = transpile(qc, backend, optimization_level=level)
    print(f"Level {level}: {tc.depth()} depth, {tc.size()} gates")

lessons.title: Optimization Levels
lessons.content:
Optimization Levels Deep Dive

🔬 Hands-On Lab

Experiment with different transpiler optimization levels and see their impact on circuit depth, gate count, and execution quality.

Understanding Optimization Passes

Each optimization level applies different transformation passes to your circuit:

Level Passes Applied Use Case
0 Basis translation, layout only Debugging, preserving structure
1 + Light optimization, 1Q gate merging Default, good balance
2 + Commutation analysis, noise-aware Better fidelity needed
3 + Heavy resynthesis, unitary optimization Maximum optimization

Practical Comparison

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
import time

# Create a complex circuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(4)
for i in range(4):
    qc.h(i)
for i in range(3):
    qc.cx(i, i+1)
qc.ccx(0, 1, 3)
qc.measure_all()

backend = AerSimulator()

print(f"Original: depth={qc.depth()}, gates={qc.size()}\n")

for level in [0, 1, 2, 3]:
    start = time.time()
    tc = transpile(qc, backend, optimization_level=level)
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"Level {level}: depth={tc.depth():3d}, gates={tc.size():3d}, time={elapsed:.3f}s")

Custom Pass Manager

from qiskit.transpiler import PassManager
from qiskit.transpiler.passes import (
    Optimize1qGates,
    CXCancellation,
    RemoveBarriers
)

# Build custom optimization pipeline
pm = PassManager([
    RemoveBarriers(),
    Optimize1qGates(),
    CXCancellation(),
])

# Apply custom passes
optimized = pm.run(qc)
print(optimized.draw())
keyTakeaways: Level 0: Minimal transformation, preserves circuit structure
Level 1: Default, balances optimization time and quality
Level 2: Better results for noisy hardware
Level 3: Maximum optimization, longest compile time
Custom PassManager allows fine-grained control

codeExamples.code:
from qiskit.transpiler import PassManager
from qiskit.transpiler.passes import Optimize1qGates, CXCancellation

pm = PassManager([Optimize1qGates(), CXCancellation()])
optimized = pm.run(circuit)
codeExamples.explanation: Creating a custom optimization pass manager

lessons.title: Noise Models
lessons.content:
Noise Models in Qiskit

💡 Why Noise Modeling?

Real quantum computers are noisy. Understanding and simulating noise helps you design more robust algorithms and estimate real-world performance.

Types of Quantum Noise

Gate Errors

Imperfect gate operations that don't perform exactly as intended.

  • Depolarizing noise
  • Coherent errors
  • Over/under rotation

Decoherence

Quantum states losing coherence over time.

  • T1 (amplitude damping)
  • T2 (phase damping)
  • Thermal relaxation

Building a Noise Model

from qiskit_aer.noise import NoiseModel, depolarizing_error

# Create empty noise model
noise_model = NoiseModel()

# Add depolarizing error to single-qubit gates
error_1q = depolarizing_error(0.01, 1)  # 1% error
noise_model.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(error_1q, ['x', 'h', 'rz'])

# Add depolarizing error to two-qubit gates (higher error)
error_2q = depolarizing_error(0.02, 2)  # 2% error
noise_model.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(error_2q, ['cx'])

print(noise_model)

Running with Noise

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator

# Create Bell state
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure_all()

# Ideal simulation
ideal_sim = AerSimulator()
ideal_result = ideal_sim.run(transpile(qc, ideal_sim), shots=10000).result()
print("Ideal:", ideal_result.get_counts())

# Noisy simulation
noisy_sim = AerSimulator(noise_model=noise_model)
noisy_result = noisy_sim.run(transpile(qc, noisy_sim), shots=10000).result()
print("Noisy:", noisy_result.get_counts())

Thermal Relaxation

from qiskit_aer.noise import thermal_relaxation_error

# Typical IBM quantum computer values
T1 = 50e-6  # 50 microseconds
T2 = 70e-6  # 70 microseconds
gate_time = 50e-9  # 50 nanoseconds

# Create thermal relaxation error
thermal_error = thermal_relaxation_error(T1, T2, gate_time)

noise_model = NoiseModel()
noise_model.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(thermal_error, ['x', 'h'])
keyTakeaways: Real quantum hardware has gate errors and decoherence
Depolarizing noise models random gate errors
T1/T2 times characterize how long qubits maintain coherence
Noise simulation helps predict real hardware behavior

codeExamples.code:
from qiskit_aer.noise import NoiseModel, depolarizing_error

noise = NoiseModel()
noise.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(depolarizing_error(0.01, 1), ['h', 'x'])
noise.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(depolarizing_error(0.02, 2), ['cx'])
codeExamples.explanation: Creating a basic depolarizing noise model

lessons.title: Error Mitigation Techniques
lessons.content:
Error Mitigation Techniques

🔬 Hands-On Lab

Learn practical techniques to reduce the impact of noise on your quantum computations without full error correction.

Error Mitigation vs Error Correction

Error Mitigation

  • Post-processing techniques
  • No extra qubits needed
  • Improves expectation values
  • Available NOW

Error Correction

  • Encodes logical qubits
  • Requires many physical qubits
  • Full fault tolerance
  • Future technology

1. Measurement Error Mitigation

from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService, Sampler, Options

# Enable measurement error mitigation
options = Options()
options.resilience_level = 1  # Enables M3 mitigation

sampler = Sampler(backend, options=options)
job = sampler.run(circuit)
result = job.result()

2. Zero Noise Extrapolation (ZNE)

Run the circuit at different noise levels and extrapolate to zero noise:

# Conceptual ZNE implementation
def amplify_noise(circuit, factor):
    """Amplify noise by repeating gates"""
    amplified = circuit.copy()
    # For factor=3: replace each CX with CX-CX-CX
    return amplified

# Run at different noise levels
results = []
for factor in [1, 2, 3]:
    amp_circuit = amplify_noise(circuit, factor)
    result = backend.run(amp_circuit).result()
    results.append(result)

# Extrapolate to zero noise
zero_noise_result = extrapolate(results)

3. Twirled Readout Error Extinction (TREX)

# Using IBM Runtime with resilience options
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import Options

options = Options()
options.resilience_level = 2  # Includes ZNE
options.resilience.noise_factors = [1, 3, 5]
options.resilience.extrapolator = 'linear'

estimator = Estimator(backend, options=options)
result = estimator.run(circuit, observable).result()
keyTakeaways: Error mitigation improves results without extra qubits
Measurement mitigation corrects readout errors
ZNE extrapolates to zero noise from amplified results
IBM Runtime provides built-in mitigation via resilience_level

codeExamples.code:
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import Options

options = Options()
options.resilience_level = 2  # Enable error mitigation
options.resilience.noise_factors = [1, 3, 5]
codeExamples.explanation: Configuring error mitigation in IBM Runtime

lessons.title: Statevector vs QASM Simulation
lessons.content:
Statevector vs QASM Simulation

🔬 Hands-On Lab

Understand the difference between statevector (exact) and QASM (sampling) simulation methods.

Comparison

Aspect Statevector QASM
Output Exact quantum state Measurement counts
Memory 2^n complex numbers O(shots)
Max qubits ~30-35 qubits Can be higher
Use case Algorithm verification Statistical results

Statevector Simulation

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector

# Create circuit WITHOUT measurement
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)

# Get exact statevector
state = Statevector.from_instruction(qc)
print(state.draw('text'))
# Output: [0.707, 0, 0, 0.707]
# This is (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2

# Get probabilities
probs = state.probabilities_dict()
print(probs)  # {'00': 0.5, '11': 0.5}

QASM Simulation

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator

# Create circuit WITH measurement
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])

# Run QASM simulation
sim = AerSimulator(method='automatic')  # Uses QASM for measured circuits
job = sim.run(transpile(qc, sim), shots=10000)
counts = job.result().get_counts()

print(counts)  # {'00': 4987, '11': 5013}

When to Use Each

Use Statevector When:

  • Debugging algorithms
  • Verifying exact states
  • Computing fidelity
  • Small circuits (< 30 qubits)

Use QASM When:

  • Mimicking real hardware
  • Testing with noise
  • Statistical analysis
  • Larger circuits
keyTakeaways: Statevector gives exact quantum state (no measurement)
QASM gives measurement statistics (like real hardware)
Statevector: exponential memory, limited qubits
QASM: sampling-based, can handle noise models

codeExamples.code:
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector

state = Statevector.from_instruction(circuit)
print(state.draw('text'))
print(state.probabilities_dict())
codeExamples.explanation: Getting the exact statevector and probabilities

lessons.title: Visualization Tools
lessons.content:
Qiskit Visualization Tools

🔬 Hands-On Lab

Master Qiskit's powerful visualization tools for circuits, states, and results.

Circuit Visualization

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.cx(1, 2)
qc.measure_all()

# Text drawing (works everywhere)
print(qc.draw('text'))

# Matplotlib (for notebooks/saving)
qc.draw('mpl', filename='circuit.png')

# LaTeX (publication quality)
qc.draw('latex_source')

State Visualization

from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
from qiskit.visualization import plot_bloch_multivector, plot_state_city

# Create a state
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
state = Statevector.from_instruction(qc)

# Bloch sphere visualization
plot_bloch_multivector(state)

# City plot (amplitude bars)
plot_state_city(state)

# Hinton diagram
plot_state_hinton(state)

Results Visualization

from qiskit.visualization import plot_histogram

# After running a circuit
counts = {'00': 500, '11': 500}

# Simple histogram
plot_histogram(counts)

# Compare multiple results
counts_ideal = {'00': 512, '11': 512}
counts_noisy = {'00': 480, '01': 30, '10': 25, '11': 465}
plot_histogram([counts_ideal, counts_noisy], 
               legend=['Ideal', 'Noisy'],
               title='Bell State Results')

Gate and Error Visualization

from qiskit.visualization import plot_gate_map, plot_error_map

# Visualize backend topology
backend = service.backend('ibm_kyoto')
plot_gate_map(backend)

# Show error rates on the map
plot_error_map(backend)
keyTakeaways: circuit.draw() supports text, mpl, and latex formats
plot_bloch_multivector shows qubit states on Bloch spheres
plot_histogram compares measurement results
plot_gate_map/plot_error_map visualize backend topology

codeExamples.code:
from qiskit.visualization import plot_histogram, plot_bloch_multivector

# Histogram
plot_histogram(counts)

# Bloch sphere
plot_bloch_multivector(statevector)

lessons.title: Primitives: Sampler & Estimator
lessons.content:
Primitives: Sampler & Estimator

🔬 Hands-On Lab

Learn the modern Qiskit Primitives API - the recommended way to run quantum circuits in Qiskit 1.0+.

What are Primitives?

Primitives are high-level interfaces that abstract circuit execution. They handle transpilation, execution, and result processing automatically.

Sampler

Returns quasi-probability distributions from circuit measurements.

Use for: Sampling, optimization, machine learning

Estimator

Computes expectation values of observables.

Use for: VQE, QAOA, quantum chemistry

Using Sampler

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.primitives import StatevectorSampler

# Create circuit with measurements
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure_all()

# Run with Sampler
sampler = StatevectorSampler()
job = sampler.run([qc], shots=1000)
result = job.result()

# Get quasi-probability distribution
pub_result = result[0]
print(pub_result.data.meas.get_counts())
# {'00': 500, '11': 500}

Using Estimator

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.primitives import StatevectorEstimator
from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp

# Create circuit WITHOUT measurement
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)

# Define observable (ZZ measurement)
observable = SparsePauliOp(['ZZ'])

# Run with Estimator
estimator = StatevectorEstimator()
job = estimator.run([(qc, observable)])
result = job.result()

# Get expectation value
print(f"⟨ZZ⟩ = {result[0].data.evs[0]}")
# Expected: 1.0 for Bell state

IBM Runtime Primitives

from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService, SamplerV2, EstimatorV2

# Connect to IBM Quantum
service = QiskitRuntimeService()
backend = service.least_busy(operational=True, simulator=False)

# Use Runtime Sampler (runs on real hardware)
sampler = SamplerV2(backend)
job = sampler.run([circuit])
result = job.result()

# Use Runtime Estimator
estimator = EstimatorV2(backend)
job = estimator.run([(circuit, observable)])
result = job.result()
keyTakeaways: Primitives are the modern API for circuit execution
Sampler returns measurement distributions
Estimator computes expectation values of observables
IBM Runtime Primitives add error mitigation and hardware access

codeExamples.code:
from qiskit.primitives import StatevectorSampler

sampler = StatevectorSampler()
result = sampler.run([circuit], shots=1000).result()
print(result[0].data.meas.get_counts())

lessons.title: Qiskit SDK Quiz
lessons.content:
Qiskit SDK Deep Dive - Quiz

📝 Knowledge Check

Test your understanding of the Qiskit SDK concepts covered in this track.

Question 1

What is the purpose of transpilation in Qiskit?

A) To convert Python to quantum assembly
B) To optimize circuits for specific backend constraints ✓
C) To simulate quantum noise
D) To visualize quantum circuits

Question 2

Which primitive should you use to compute ⟨ψ|H|ψ⟩ (expectation value)?

A) Sampler
B) Estimator ✓
C) AerSimulator
D) Transpiler

Question 3

What does optimization_level=3 in transpile() do?

A) Fastest compilation, no optimization
B) Default balanced optimization
C) Maximum optimization with longest compile time ✓
D) Only applies noise mitigation

Question 4

What is the key difference between Statevector and QASM simulation?

A) Statevector gives exact state, QASM gives measurement samples ✓
B) QASM is faster than Statevector
C) Statevector can handle more qubits
D) There is no difference
keyTakeaways: Transpilation optimizes circuits for hardware constraints
Estimator computes expectation values, Sampler returns distributions
optimization_level=3 provides maximum circuit optimization
Statevector is exact, QASM simulates measurement sampling
